nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-01.title: Eliminate the other digits
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-01.body:
The number has one $m$, then a $3$, then $19$ more $m$'s.

- If $m$ is even, the number is even.
- If $m=5$, it ends in $5$.
- If $m=3$ or $m=9$, every digit is a multiple of $3$, so the number is divisible by $3$.
- If $m=7$, counting from the right, the digits in odd positions are eleven $7$'s (sum $77$) and the digits in even positions are nine $7$'s and the $3$ (sum $66$). The difference is $11$, so the number is divisible by $11$.

So $m=1$, and indeed $1311\ldots1$ is prime.

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-02.title: Bound the digits
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-02.body:
No digit can exceed $6$, since $7!>999$. A digit $6$ is also impossible: $6!=720$ would force a hundreds digit of at least $7$.

If no digit is $5$, the sum is at most $3\cdot4!=72<100$. Three $5$'s give $360\ne555$, and two $5$'s give $240+a!$ with $a\le4$, which never contains two $5$'s. So there is exactly one $5$, the sum is between $120+2=122$ and $120+48=168$, and the hundreds digit is $1$.

Testing $\overline{1a5}$ and $\overline{15a}$ for $a\in\{0,\dots,4\}$: $1!+4!+5!=145$ works.

**Answer: 145**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-03.title: Determine the floor values
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-03.body: Let $a=\lfloor x+20\rfloor$ and $b=\lfloor x+14\rfloor$. For non-integer $x$, $b=a-6$; for integer $x$, $b=a-6$ as well. The product $a(a-6)$ is prime iff one factor is $\pm1$ and the other is a prime of the same sign. $a-6=1\Rightarrow a=7$: product $=7$ (prime ✓), $a=\lfloor x+20\rfloor=7$ means $x\in[-13,-12)$. $a=-1$: product $=(-1)(-7)=7$ (prime ✓), $a=\lfloor x+20\rfloor=-1$ means $x\in[-21,-20)$. Answer: $x\in[-13,-12)\cup[-21,-20)$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-04.title: Factorize 25 with four distinct integers
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-04.body:
If $r$ is the integer root, then $(r-a)(r-b)(r-c)(r-d)=25$ with four distinct integer factors. The only possibility is $\{r-a,r-b,r-c,r-d\}=\{1,-1,5,-5\}$.

Now $a-b+c-d=-(r-a)+(r-b)-(r-c)+(r-d)$, which is largest when $r-a$ and $r-c$ are the negative factors: $-(-5)+5-(-1)+1=12$.

**Answer: 12**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-06.title: Coordinate geometry
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-06.body: Place $A=(0,0)$, equilateral $\triangle ABC$ with $B=(-7,-7\sqrt3)$, $C=(7,-7\sqrt3)$. Line $BC$ is $y=-7\sqrt3$. With $AD=20$: $D=(\sqrt{253},-7\sqrt3)$. Rotating $D$ around $A$ by $+60°$ gives $E=\left(\frac{\sqrt{253}+7}{2},\frac{\sqrt3(\sqrt{253}+7)}{2}\right)$. Then $CE=\sqrt{\left(\frac{\sqrt{253}+7}{2}-7\right)^2+\left(\frac{\sqrt3(\sqrt{253}+7)}{2}\right)^2}=\sqrt{(\sqrt{253}+7)^2}=7+\sqrt{253}$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-08.title: Recognize the tangent subtraction formula
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-08.body: $\dfrac{\cos x-\sin x}{\cos x+\sin x}=\dfrac{1-\tan x}{1+\tan x}=\tan(45°-x)$. So $\tan20°=\tan(45°-x)$, giving $20°=45°-x$, $x=25°$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-09.title: Telescoping product
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-09.body: Each factor $(1+10^k+10^{2k})=\dfrac{10^{3k}-1}{10^k-1}$. The product telescopes to $\dfrac{10^{81}-1}{10^1-1}=\underbrace{11\cdots1}_{81}$ (81 ones). Digit sum $=81$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-10.title: Coordinates
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-10.body: Place $B=(0,0)$, $C=(11,0)$. By the cosine rule $\cos B=\frac{81+121-100}{198}=\frac{17}{33}$, so $\sin B=\frac{20\sqrt2}{33}$ and $A=\left(\frac{51}{11},\frac{60\sqrt2}{11}\right)$. The angle bisector gives $D=\left(\frac{15}{2},3\sqrt2\right)$ on $AC$ (using $AD/DC=9/11$). $E$ on line $BD$ with $CE\perp BD$: parameterize $BD$ as $t\cdot D$, set $(E-C)\cdot D=0$, solve to get $t=10/9$, $E=\left(\frac{25}{3},\frac{10\sqrt2}{3}\right)$. Area of $\triangle ABE=\frac{1}{2}|{(B-A)\times(E-A)}|=15\sqrt2$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-12.title: Roots of unity
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-12.body: $z=e^{2\pi ik/12}$, $w=e^{2\pi im/15}$. The product $zw=e^{2\pi i(5k+4m)/60}$. Since $\gcd(5,4)=1$, the set $\{5k+4m\pmod{60}\}$ generates all residues mod 60. So there are 60 distinct values.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-14.title: Compute period of 3 mod 100
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-14.body: The last two digits of powers of 3 have period 20. $2014\equiv14\pmod{20}$. Computing: $3^{14}=4782969$, last two digits $69$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-16.title: Telescoping
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-16.body: $a_n=n^3-(n-1)^3=3n^2-3n+1$. So $a_n-1=3n(n-1)$. By partial fractions: $\frac{1}{a_n-1}=\frac{1}{3n(n-1)}=\frac{1}{3}\left(\frac{1}{n-1}-\frac{1}{n}\right)$. Sum from $n=2$ to $2014$: $\frac{1}{3}\left(1-\frac{1}{2014}\right)=\frac{2013}{3\times2014}=\frac{671}{2014}$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-17.title: Always possible to form a triangle
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-17.body:
If the point is $(x,y)$, the four sticks have lengths $x,\,1-x,\,y,\,1-y$. If $x$ is the shortest stick, then $1-x$ is the longest (every stick is the complement of another), and similarly for the others. So if the lengths are $0<a\le b\le c\le d$, then $a+d=1=b+c$.

Since $a>0$, we get $b+c=a+d>d$, so the sticks $b,c,d$ always form a triangle. The probability is $1$.

**Answer: 1**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-18.title: Similar triangles
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-18.body:
Since $AE$ bisects $\angle A$ and $m\angle BAE=14^\circ$, $m\angle BAD=28^\circ$.

In $\triangle BCE$, $BE=EC$ gives $m\angle ECB=m\angle EBC=14^\circ$, so $m\angle BEC=152^\circ$ and $m\angle CED=28^\circ=m\angle BAD$.

By the angle bisector theorem in $\triangle ABD$, $\dfrac{AB}{AD}=\dfrac{BE}{ED}=\dfrac{CE}{DE}$. Together with $m\angle BAD=m\angle CED$, this gives $\triangle ABD\sim\triangle ECD$ (SAS), so $m\angle CDE=m\angle BDA$.

In $\triangle ABD$, $m\angle BDA=180^\circ-20^\circ-28^\circ=132^\circ$. Hence $m\angle D=m\angle ADB+m\angle BDC=132^\circ+132^\circ=264^\circ$ (the quadrilateral is not convex).

**Answer: 264°**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-19.title: Bound from Thursday and Friday
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-19.body:
No student attended both Thursday and Friday, so there are at least $14+20=34$ students.

$34$ is enough: let $17$ of the Friday students also attend Monday and $16$ of them also attend Wednesday, and let $12$ of the Thursday students also attend Tuesday. No one attends two consecutive days.

**Answer: 34**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-20.title: Prime factorization and divisors
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-20.body: $2014^3=(2\cdot19\cdot53)^3=2^3\cdot19^3\cdot53^3$. For each prime $p^k$, the number of ways to distribute the exponent among $a,b,c$ is $\binom{k+2}{2}=\binom{5}{2}=10$. Total ordered triples $=10^3=1000$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-21.title: Angle chasing
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-21.body:
Let $m\angle DBE=x$ and $m\angle EBC=y$. Since $AB=AC$, $m\angle C=m\angle ABC=x+y$. Since $BD=DE$, $m\angle DEB=x$, and since $\angle DEC=90^\circ$, $m\angle BEC=90^\circ-x$.

The angles of $\triangle BEC$ give $y+(90^\circ-x)+(x+y)=180^\circ$, so $y=45^\circ$.

**Answer: 45°**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-22.title: Work modulo 8
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-22.body:
Each number ends in $0$: $211^{19}+9\equiv1+9$, $9^{101}-9\equiv9-9$, and $19^{111}-9\equiv9-9\pmod{10}$. So each has at least one trailing zero, and the number of trailing zeros is at most the exponent of $2$.

Modulo $8$:
- $211^{19}+9\equiv3^{19}+9\equiv3+1=4$, so it has exactly two factors of $2$: at most $2$ trailing zeros.
- $19^{111}-9\equiv3^{111}-1\equiv3-1=2$, so it has exactly one factor of $2$: exactly $1$ trailing zero.
- $9^{101}-9\equiv1-1=0$.

Since $N(A),N(B),N(C)$ are distinct, $N(19^{111}-9)=1$, $N(211^{19}+9)=2$, and $N(9^{101}-9)\ge3$.

**Answer: $(19^{111}-9,\ 211^{19}+9,\ 9^{101}-9)$**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-23.title: Two cases: A=B or A+B=90°
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-23.body:
$\sin2A=\sin2B$ gives $A=B$ or $A+B=90°$.

Case $A=B$: the sides opposite $A$ and $B$ are equal. With sides 8, 17, $c$: if $c=17$, triangle $8,17,17$ ✓; if $c=8$, triangle $8,8,17$ fails triangle inequality. Valid: $c=17$.

Case $A+B=90°$: $C=90°$. If 8 and 17 are legs: $c=\sqrt{64+289}=\sqrt{353}$ ✓. If 17 is hypotenuse: $c=\sqrt{289-64}=15$ ✓.

All possible third sides: $15$, $17$, $\sqrt{353}$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-24.title: Vieta's formulas
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-24.body:
Let the roots be $r_1,r_2$. Then $r_1+r_2=-p$ and $r_1r_2=-330p$. If one root is an integer, so is the other, and $p\mid r_1r_2$ means $p$ divides one root, hence both (by the sum). Write $r_1=py$ and $r_2=-p(y+1)$; then $-p^2y(y+1)=-330p$, so $py(y+1)=330$.

Thus $p\mid330=2\cdot3\cdot5\cdot11$. Then $y(y+1)=165,110,66,30$ for $p=2,3,5,11$; only $110=10\cdot11$ and $30=5\cdot6$ are products of consecutive integers. So $p=3$ (roots $30,-33$) or $p=11$ (roots $55,-66$), each with exactly one positive root.

**Answer: $3$ and $11$**

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-25.title: Divisibility by 4 depends on last two digits
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-25.body: A number is divisible by 4 iff its last two digits form a multiple of 4. The last two digits (each from $\{1,2,3,4,5\}$) can be any of $5^2=25$ pairs. Multiples of 4 in $\{11,...,55\}$ using only digits 1–5: 12, 24, 32, 44, 52 — 5 pairs. Probability $=5/25=1/5$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-26.title: Use complementary digit count
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-26.body: The number of digits of $n$ is $\lfloor\log_{10}n\rfloor+1$. Since $2^{2014}\times5^{2014}=10^{2014}$, we have $\log_{10}(2^{2014})+\log_{10}(5^{2014})=2014$. With $2^{2014}$ having 607 digits: $\lfloor\log_{10}(2^{2014})\rfloor=606$. The fractional part of $\log_{10}(5^{2014})$ is $1$ minus the fractional part of $\log_{10}(2^{2014})$ (since their logs sum to an integer), so $\lfloor\log_{10}(5^{2014})\rfloor=2014-606-1=1407$, giving $5^{2014}$ exactly $1408$ digits.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-29.title: Incenter angle formula
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-29.body: $F$ is the incenter. The angle at the incenter between two angle bisectors: $\angle BFA=90°+\frac{\angle C}{2}=90°+18°=108°$.

nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-30.title: Substitute t=7^x
nyciml-2013-14-spring-seniora-30.body: Let $t=7^x>0$: $at^2-7t+1=0$. Exactly one positive root when: (1) $a=0$: $t=1/7>0$ (one solution ✓); (2) $a<0$: product of roots $=1/a<0$, so roots have opposite signs — exactly one positive root ✓; (3) discriminant $=0$: $a=49/4$, double root $t=7/(2a)=2/7>0$ ✓. Answer: $a\le0$ or $a=49/4$.
